meter.definition: The base unit of length in the International System of Units (SI). Defined by setting the speed of light in vacuum to exactly 299,792,458 m/s.
meter.history: Originally defined in 1793 as 1/10,000,000 of the distance from the Earth's equator to the North Pole along a meridian through Paris.
meter.used_for: Room measurements, height, athletic tracks, and scientific spatial dimensions.
examples: Height of a standard door frame (~2 meters)
Length of an Olympic swimming pool (50 meters)

kilometer.definition: A unit of length equal to 1,000 meters.
kilometer.history: Adopted alongside the metric system during the French Revolution to standardise geography and transport measurements.
kilometer.used_for: Highway distances, geographical mapping, running races, and flight paths.
examples: A standard 5K road race (5 km)
Distance from London to Paris (~340 km)

centimeter.definition: A unit of length equal to 1/100th of a meter (0.01 m).
centimeter.history: Part of the centimetre-gram-second (CGS) system introduced by the British Association for the Advancement of Science in 1873.
centimeter.used_for: Tailoring, clothing sizing, human height, and small object measurements.
examples: Width of a standard credit card (~8.5 cm)
Diameter of a US penny (~1.9 cm)

millimeter.definition: A unit of length equal to 1/1,000th of a meter (0.001 m).
millimeter.history: Standardised as part of the SI metric scale for precision manufacturing and engineering tolerances.
millimeter.used_for: Rainfall measurement, mechanical engineering, hardware screw sizes, and paper thickness.
examples: Thickness of a standard credit card (~0.76 mm)
Diameter of a small paperclip wire (~1 mm)

micrometer.definition: A unit of length equal to 1/1,000,000th of a meter (10⁻⁶ m), also known as a micron.
micrometer.history: Coined in 1868 to describe biological cell structures observed under early compound optical microscopes.
micrometer.used_for: Cell biology, airborne particulate matter (PM2.5), semiconductor manufacturing, and textile fiber diameter.
examples: Width of a human hair (~70 μm)
Diameter of a human red blood cell (~7–8 μm)

nanometer.definition: A unit of length equal to 1/1,000,000,000th of a meter (10⁻⁹ m).
nanometer.history: Formally adopted by IUPAC and BIPM as nanotechnology and quantum optics advanced in the mid-20th century.
nanometer.used_for: Wavelengths of visible light, semiconductor transistor node sizing, and molecular biology.
examples: Wavelength of green light (~532 nm)
Width of a double-stranded DNA helix (~2 nm)

inch.definition: A unit of length equal to 2.54 centimeters in the imperial and US customary systems.
inch.history: Historically defined as the length of three dried barleycorns laid end-to-end; standardized internationally in 1959.
inch.used_for: Screen display sizes, rainfall, pipe diameters, display resolution (DPI), and carpentry.
examples: Smartphone screen diagonal size (e.g. 6.1 inches)
Standard letter paper width (8.5 inches)

foot.definition: A unit of length equal to 12 inches or 0.3048 meters.
foot.history: Based on average human foot proportions across ancient Mesopotamian, Greek, and Roman cultures.
foot.used_for: Aviation altitudes, human height in US/UK, and building floor elevations.
examples: Cruising altitude of commercial airliners (~35,000 feet)
Average height of an adult human (~5 ft 9 in)

yard.definition: A unit of length equal to 3 feet or 36 inches (0.9144 meters).
yard.history: Legend holds King Henry I of England defined the yard as the distance from his nose to the tip of his outstretched thumb.
yard.used_for: American football field markings, fabric rolls, landscaping, and golf course distances.
examples: Length of an American football field end-zone to end-zone (100 yards)
Standard fabric bolt width

mile.definition: A unit of distance equal to 5,280 feet, 1,760 yards, or 1,609.344 meters.
mile.history: Derived from the Roman 'mille passus', meaning 1,000 double-steps of a marching Roman legion.
mile.used_for: Highway speed limits, long-distance road trips, and marathon races.
examples: Official marathon race distance (26.2 miles)
Distance traveled driving at 60 mph for one hour

nautical mile.definition: A unit of distance based on one minute of arc along a meridian of the Earth, equal to exactly 1,852 meters.
nautical mile.history: Developed by Renaissance navigators correlating terrestrial map coordinates directly with celestial navigation.
nautical mile.used_for: Maritime navigation, international aviation, and territorial water boundaries.
examples: Distance equivalent to 1 knot traveled over one hour
Standard international maritime boundary (12 nmi zone)

light-year.definition: The distance light travels in a vacuum in one Julian year (365.25 days), equal to ~9.461 trillion kilometers.
light-year.history: First used by German astronomer Friedrich Bessel in 1838 after successfully calculating the parallax of 61 Cygni.
light-year.used_for: Interstellar and galactic distance measurements in astronomy and astrophysics.
examples: Distance to Proxima Centauri, nearest star to Sun (~4.24 light-years)
Diameter of the Milky Way galaxy (~100,000 light-years)

astronomical unit.definition: A unit of length defined as exactly 149,597,870,700 meters (~150 million km), roughly Earth's average distance to the Sun.
astronomical unit.history: Calculated by Giovanni Cassini in 1672 using Mars parallax measurements between Paris and French Guiana.
astronomical unit.used_for: Measuring distances within the Solar System and planetary orbits.
examples: Distance from Earth to the Sun (1 AU)
Distance from Sun to Neptune (~30 AU)

parsec.definition: A unit of astronomical length equal to approximately 3.26 light-years or 30.9 trillion kilometers.
parsec.history: Coined in 1913 by British astronomer Herbert Hall Turner from 'parallax of one arcsecond'.
parsec.used_for: Extra-solar star distances, galactic clusters, and cosmological scale mapping.
examples: Distance from Sun to Proxima Centauri (~1.3 parsecs)
Distance to the center of the Milky Way (~8,000 parsecs)

kilogram.definition: The SI base unit of mass. Defined by fixing Planck's constant h to 6.62607015×10⁻³⁴ J·s.
kilogram.history: Redefined in 2019 away from the physical artifact cylinder 'Le Grand K' kept in Sèvres, France.
kilogram.used_for: Human body weight, luggage limits, commercial freight, and grocery produce.
examples: Weight of a standard 1-liter bottle of water (1 kg)
Average birth weight of a newborn (~3.5 kg)

gram.definition: A unit of mass equal to 1/1,000th of a kilogram (0.001 kg).
gram.history: Originally defined in 1795 as the absolute mass of 1 cubic centimeter of pure water at melting ice temperature.
gram.used_for: Nutritional labels, baking ingredients, precious metals, and pharmacy dosages.
examples: Mass of a standard metal paperclip (~1 gram)
Mass of a US 1-dollar bill (~1 gram)

milligram.definition: A unit of mass equal to 1/1,000th of a gram (10⁻⁶ kg).
milligram.history: Standardised under SI metric prefixes for chemistry, analytical toxicology, and medical formulation.
milligram.used_for: Pharmaceutical active drug ingredients, dietary vitamin supplements, and blood chemistry lab reports.
examples: Standard adult aspirin tablet dose (325 mg)
Caffeine content in a typical cup of coffee (~95 mg)

microgram.definition: A unit of mass equal to 1/1,000,000th of a gram (10⁻⁹ kg).
microgram.history: Essential in biochemistry and endocrinology for quantifying hormone levels and trace micronutrients.
microgram.used_for: Trace vitamins (Vitamin D, B12), potent prescription medication doses, and hormone diagnostics.
examples: Recommended daily Vitamin D intake (~15–20 μg)
Weight of a single pollen grain (~1–5 μg)

metric ton.definition: A unit of mass equal to 1,000 kilograms or ~2,204.62 pounds, also called a tonne.
metric ton.history: Adopted internationally to simplify maritime cargo tonnage and heavy industrial transport.
metric ton.used_for: Industrial steel production, shipping container capacity, crop yields, and vehicle weight.
examples: Weight of an average adult female African elephant (~3–4 metric tons)
Weight of a compact passenger car (~1.2 to 1.5 metric tons)

pound.definition: A unit of mass equal to 16 ounces or exactly 0.45359237 kilograms.
pound.history: Derived from the Roman 'libra pondo', which supplied both the symbol 'lb' and word 'pound'.
pound.used_for: Human body weight in US/UK, commercial meat produce, and shipping parcels.
examples: Weight of a standard loaf of bread (~1 pound)
Weight of a professional bowling ball (10 to 16 lbs)

ounce.definition: A unit of mass equal to 1/16th of a pound or ~28.3495 grams.
ounce.history: Traced to the Roman 'uncia', denoting one-twelfth of an as (ancient unit of weight).
ounce.used_for: Postal letter limits, food portioning, packaged snack weights, and yarn weight.
examples: Weight of a single slice of cheddar cheese (~1 oz)
Weight limit for standard first-class postage (~1 oz)

stone.definition: An imperial unit of mass equal to 14 pounds or approximately 6.35029 kilograms.
stone.history: Historically derived from standardized stone weights used in agricultural markets across northern Europe.
stone.used_for: Human body weight measurement commonly used in the UK and Ireland.
examples: Average weight of an adult human male (~12 to 14 stone)
Weight of a 70 kg person (~11 st 0 lb)

carat.definition: A unit of mass equal to 200 milligrams (0.2 grams), used exclusively for gemstones and pearls.
carat.history: Derived from carob seeds ('kuárem' in Greek), which were historically prized for their consistent mass.
carat.used_for: Weight measurement of diamonds, rubies, emeralds, sapphires, and natural pearls.
examples: Average size of a solitaire diamond engagement ring (~1.0 carat / 0.2 g)
Mass of the famous Hope Diamond (45.52 carats)

atomic mass unit.definition: A unit of mass defined as 1/12th of the mass of an unbound neutral carbon-12 atom at rest (~1.66054×10⁻²⁷ kg).
atomic mass unit.history: Standardized by IUPAP in 1961 to unify chemical mass scales based on oxygen with physical mass scales.
atomic mass unit.used_for: Masses of atoms, isotopes, subatomic particles, and molecular weight in chemistry.
examples: Mass of a single hydrogen atom (~1.008 u)
Mass of a carbon-12 nucleus (exactly 12 u)

celsius.definition: A temperature scale where 0 °C is the freezing point of water and 100 °C is the boiling point at 1 atm.
celsius.history: Invented by Swedish astronomer Anders Celsius in 1742, originally inverted with 0 °C as boiling point.
celsius.used_for: Everyday weather, medical diagnostics, room comfort, and scientific research globally.
examples: Normal human body temperature (37 °C)
Comfortable indoor room temperature (20–22 °C)

fahrenheit.definition: A temperature scale where water freezes at 32 °F and boils at 212 °F under 1 atm pressure.
fahrenheit.history: Proposed in 1724 by physicist Daniel Gabriel Fahrenheit using an ice-water-brine mixture as 0 °F reference.
fahrenheit.used_for: Weather forecasts, household thermostats, and culinary baking in the United States.
examples: Standard oven baking temperature (~350 °F)
Hot summer afternoon (90–100 °F)

kelvin.definition: The SI base unit of thermodynamic temperature. 0 K represents absolute zero (zero molecular kinetic energy).
kelvin.history: Proposed by Lord Kelvin in 1848 based on thermodynamic laws independent of specific substance properties.
kelvin.used_for: Cryogenics, astrophysics, physical chemistry, and lighting color temperature.
examples: Melting point of ice (273.15 K)
Warm white LED light bulb color temperature (~2700–3000 K)

rankine.definition: An absolute thermodynamic temperature scale using Fahrenheit degree intervals, where 0 °R = absolute zero.
rankine.history: Proposed by Scottish engineer William John Macquorn Rankine in 1859 for thermodynamic calculations.
rankine.used_for: Aerospace engineering and thermal energy calculations in US engineering industries.
examples: Freezing point of water (491.67 °R)
Standard room temperature (~536.67 °R)

square meter.definition: The SI derived unit of area, equal to the area of a square with sides of 1 meter in length.
square meter.history: Established with the French metric reform in 1795 as the foundation for spatial measurement.
square meter.used_for: Real estate floor plans, apartment areas, carpet laying, and land surveying.
examples: Floor area of a typical bedroom (~12–15 m²)
Area of a singles tennis court (~195 m²)

square kilometer.definition: A unit of area equal to 1,000,000 square meters (1 km × 1 km).
square kilometer.history: Adopted globally for national geographic area surveys, city footprints, and environmental mapping.
square kilometer.used_for: Country land area, national park sizes, urban sprawl, and lake surface areas.
examples: Total surface area of Central Park, New York (~3.41 km²)
Total land area of Monaco (~2.02 km²)

square foot.definition: A unit of area equal to 144 square inches or ~0.092903 square meters.
square foot.history: Standard real estate unit in imperial countries established during medieval English land tenure systems.
square foot.used_for: Residential property listings, office space leasing, and interior design planning.
examples: Floor area of a standard two-car garage (~400 sq ft)
Average size of a US single-family home (~2,300 sq ft)

square inch.definition: A unit of area equal to the area of a square with 1-inch sides (~6.4516 cm²).
square inch.history: Traditional engineering unit for stress (PSI = pounds per square inch) and cross-sectional area.
square inch.used_for: Tire pressure contact patches, mechanical piston heads, and printing resolution.
examples: Area of a standard US postage stamp (~1 sq in)
Area of a smartphone display screen (~12–15 sq in)

acre.definition: A unit of land area equal to 43,560 square feet or ~4,046.86 square meters.
acre.history: Historically defined as the amount of land executable by one yoke of oxen plowing in one day ('furlong by chain').
acre.used_for: Agricultural farmland, forest tracts, residential land lots, and real estate subdivisions.
examples: Area of an American football field excluding end-zones (~1.32 acres)
Standard 1-acre residential lot

hectare.definition: A non-SI metric unit of area equal to 10,000 square meters (100 m × 100 m) or ~2.471 acres.
hectare.history: Created in 1795 from the French 'are' (100 m²); 'hecto-are' means 100 ares.
hectare.used_for: Forestry, international agricultural statistics, city planning, and wildfire tracking.
examples: Area of an international regulation soccer pitch (~0.71 ha)
A 10-hectare agricultural farm (~24.7 acres)

square mile.definition: A unit of area equal to 640 acres or ~2.58999 square kilometers.
square mile.history: Formed the grid system basis for the US Public Land Survey System (PLSS) township sections.
square mile.used_for: County boundaries, city territorial areas, and wildlife reserve acreage.
examples: Land area of a standard US PLSS survey section (1 sq mi)
Area of Manhattan Island (~22.8 sq mi)

liter.definition: A metric unit of volume equal to 1 cubic decimeter (1,000 cubic centimeters).
liter.history: Created in France in 1795 as one of the fundamental units of the original metric system.
liter.used_for: Beverage packaging, vehicle engine displacement, fuel tanks, and fluid containers.
examples: Standard 2-liter soda bottle
Fuel tank capacity of a compact automobile (~50 liters)

milliliter.definition: A metric unit of volume equal to 1/1,000th of a liter or 1 cubic centimeter (cm³).
milliliter.history: Derived from the metric prefix 'milli-' to standardise liquid dosage and laboratory chemistry.
milliliter.used_for: Liquid medication doses, perfume bottles, beverage cans, and chemistry titrations.
examples: Standard liquid cough syrup dose (5 mL)
Standard aluminum beverage can (355 mL)

cubic meter.definition: The SI unit of volume, equal to a cube with 1-meter sides (1,000 liters).
cubic meter.history: Foundation of metric volumetric measurement defined during the 1795 French metric reform.
cubic meter.used_for: Natural gas utility billing, swimming pool volume, concrete pouring, and cargo ship capacity.
examples: Volume of an Olympic swimming pool (~2,500 m³)
Monthly household water usage (~15–20 m³)

cubic centimeter.definition: A metric unit of volume equal to 1 milliliter (1/1,000,000 of a m³), abbreviated 'cc'.
cubic centimeter.history: Core volume unit of the centimetre-gram-second (CGS) system of physical units.
cubic centimeter.used_for: Motorcycle/car engine displacement (e.g. 250cc, 2000cc), medical syringes, and material density.
examples: Engine size of a lightweight motor scooter (50 cc)
Medical injection syringe volume (3 cc)

gallon_us.definition: A US customary unit of volume equal to 128 US fluid ounces or ~3.78541 liters.
gallon_us.history: Derived from the Queen Anne wine gallon of 1707 adopted by the United States Treasury.
gallon_us.used_for: Gasoline pricing in the US, milk jugs, paint cans, and large liquid storage.
examples: Standard gallon jug of milk in US grocery stores (1 gal)
Standard paint container size (1 gallon)

gallon_uk.definition: An imperial unit of volume equal to 160 UK fluid ounces or exactly 4.54609 liters.
gallon_uk.history: Established by the British Imperial Weights and Measures Act of 1824 based on 10 lbs of water at 62 °F.
gallon_uk.used_for: Fuel efficiency ratings (MPG-UK) and liquid volume in the UK, Canada, and Caribbean.
examples: An Imperial gallon of water weighs exactly 10 lbs
Fuel efficiency comparison in UK automotive tests

fluid ounce.definition: A unit of liquid volume equal to 1/128th of a US gallon or ~29.5735 milliliters.
fluid ounce.history: Created to measure volume of liquids whose weight was roughly equal to one avoirdupois ounce of water.
fluid ounce.used_for: Beverage packaging, espresso shots, liquid medicine, and cosmetics.
examples: Standard US shot glass volume (1.5 fl oz)
Standard bottle of water (~16.9 fl oz / 500 mL)

cup.definition: A unit of volume used in cooking equal to 8 US fluid ounces or ~236.588 milliliters.
cup.history: Standardised for domestic culinary recipes by American home economist Fannie Farmer in 1896.
cup.used_for: Cooking, baking recipes, coffee maker carafes, and dietary portion control.
examples: One cup of granulated sugar (~200 grams)
A standard mug of coffee (~1 cup)

meters per second.definition: The SI derived unit of speed and velocity, equal to traveling 1 meter in 1 second.
meters per second.history: Formulated alongside Newton's laws of motion and formalised under the international metric standard.
meters per second.used_for: Physics velocity problems, wind speed in meteorology, and aerodynamics.
examples: Speed of sound in dry air at 20 °C (~343 m/s)
Sprint speed of an Olympic athlete (~10–12 m/s)

kilometers per hour.definition: A unit of speed equal to traveling 1 kilometer in 1 hour (~0.27778 m/s).
kilometers per hour.history: Adopted internationally for road transport as automobiles replaced horse-drawn carriages in metric countries.
kilometers per hour.used_for: Highway speed limits, automotive speedometers, train travel, and cycling speeds.
examples: Highway speed limit in most European countries (120 km/h)
Cruising speed of a high-speed train (300 km/h)

miles per hour.definition: A unit of speed equal to traveling 1 statute mile in 1 hour (~1.60934 km/h).
miles per hour.history: Traditional speed unit in the UK and US derived from railroad velocity tracking in the 19th century.
miles per hour.used_for: Speed limits and speedometers in the United States, United Kingdom, and Caribbean.
examples: Standard US highway speed limit (65–70 mph)
Speed of a fast baseball pitch (~95–100 mph)

knot.definition: A unit of speed equal to 1 nautical mile per hour (exactly 1.852 km/h or ~1.15078 mph).
knot.history: Named after dropping a chip log attached to a knotted rope behind a sailing ship to count knots over time.
knot.used_for: Aircraft airspeed, ship vessel cruising speeds, and ocean current tracking.
examples: Cruising speed of a commercial passenger jet (~450–500 knots)
Cruising speed of a cruise ship (~20–24 knots)

mach.definition: A dimensionless unit of speed relative to the local speed of sound in the surrounding medium.
mach.history: Named after Austrian physicist Ernst Mach, who conducted pioneering research into supersonic gas dynamics.
mach.used_for: Supersonic aircraft flight speeds, military jet aviation, and space re-entry vehicles.
examples: Mach 1 at sea level (~1,225 km/h / 761 mph)
Top speed of Concorde passenger aircraft (Mach 2.04)

second.definition: The SI base unit of time. Defined by taking the fixed numerical value of the cesium-133 hyperfine transition frequency ΔνCs as 9,192,631,770 Hz.
second.history: Originally defined as 1/86,400 of a mean solar day; redefined via atomic clocks in 1967.
second.used_for: Scientific timing, athletics, clock seconds, computing CPU clock cycles, and physics formulas.
examples: Average human heart beat duration (~0.8 to 1 second)
Duration of one second tick on a wall clock

millisecond.definition: A unit of time equal to 1/1,000th of a second (0.001 s).
millisecond.history: Essential in electrical engineering, acoustics, and high-frequency instrumentation.
millisecond.used_for: Computer monitor response time, web latency (ping), camera shutter speeds, and audio delay.
examples: Duration of a single camera shutter flash (~1–2 ms)
Human eye blink duration (~100–400 ms)

microsecond.definition: A unit of time equal to 1/1,000,000th of a second (10⁻⁶ s).
microsecond.history: Adopted in early computing and radar technology to measure pulse travel and logic gate switching times.
microsecond.used_for: Computer RAM access latency, electronic gate delays, laser pulses, and ultrasound imaging.
examples: DRAM memory chip access latency (~50–100 μs)
Time taken for light to travel 300 meters (1 μs)

nanosecond.definition: A unit of time equal to 1/1,000,000,000th of a second (10⁻⁹ s).
nanosecond.history: Popularised by computer pioneer Grace Hopper, who handed out 11.8-inch pieces of wire representing a light-nanosecond.
nanosecond.used_for: Microprocessor clock cycles (GHz), fiber optic data transmission, and particle physics.
examples: Duration of one clock cycle on a 3 GHz processor (~0.33 ns)
Distance light travels in 1 nanosecond (~30 cm / 1 foot)

minute.definition: A unit of time equal to 60 seconds.
minute.history: Derived from the Latin 'pars minuta prima', meaning first small part of an hour, traced to Babylonian sexagesimal math.
minute.used_for: Cooking timers, phone calls, sports periods, and scheduling.
examples: Time to boil a soft egg (~4–6 minutes)
Duration of a pop music song (~3–4 minutes)

hour.definition: A unit of time equal to 60 minutes or 3,600 seconds.
hour.history: Divided into 12 day hours and 12 night hours by ancient Egyptians based on sundial shadows.
hour.used_for: Work shifts, travel trip times, movie lengths, and battery endurance.
examples: Length of a typical feature film (~2 hours)
Standard daily full-time work shift (8 hours)

day.definition: A unit of time equal to 24 hours or 86,400 seconds, representing one full rotation of Earth on its axis.
day.history: Fundamental astronomical cycle recognized by all human cultures since prehistoric antiquity.
day.used_for: Calendar dates, work schedules, weather forecasts, and biological circadian cycles.
examples: Duration of one Earth axial rotation (~24 hours)
Standard weekend duration (2 days)

year.definition: A unit of time equal to 365.25 days (31,557,600 seconds), representing one complete orbital revolution of Earth around the Sun.
year.history: Standardised via the Julian (46 BC) and Gregorian (1582 AD) calendar reforms.
year.used_for: Age calculation, annual financial reports, seasonal agricultural cycles, and historical eras.
examples: Time for Earth to complete one orbit around the Sun (1 year)
Standard length of an academic school year

bit.definition: The most basic unit of digital information in computing, representing a binary state of 0 or 1.
bit.history: Coined by mathematician Claude Shannon in 1948 in his seminal paper 'A Mathematical Theory of Communication'.
bit.used_for: Network bandwidth speeds (Mbps/Gbps), binary logic, encryption key lengths (256-bit), and data compression.
examples: A single 0 or 1 state in computer memory
256-bit AES encryption key strength

byte.definition: A unit of digital data consisting of 8 bits.
byte.history: Coined by Werner Buchholz in 1956 during early IBM Stretch computer engineering to prevent text character ambiguity.
byte.used_for: Character encoding (ASCII/UTF-8), memory addressing, file sizes, and network packet headers.
examples: Storage required for a single ASCII text character (1 byte)
Short text message (~100–200 bytes)

kilobyte.definition: A unit of digital storage equal to 1,000 bytes (SI decimal) or 1,024 bytes (binary/KiB).
kilobyte.history: Commonly used in early computing (1970s–1980s) to describe floppy disk capacities and early RAM chips.
kilobyte.used_for: Plain text documents, small images, website HTML files, and low-res icons.
examples: File size of a short email message without attachments (~10–20 KB)
A small web icon image (~5 KB)

megabyte.definition: A unit of digital storage equal to 1,000,000 bytes (decimal) or 1,048,576 bytes (binary/MiB).
megabyte.history: Became the standard capacity metric during the 1990s desktop computer revolution (3.5" floppy = 1.44 MB).
megabyte.used_for: MP3 audio files, smartphone camera photos, PDF ebooks, and mobile app download sizes.
examples: Size of a high-quality 4-minute MP3 song (~8–10 MB)
High-resolution smartphone photo (~3–6 MB)

gigabyte.definition: A unit of digital storage equal to 1,000,000,000 bytes (decimal) or 1,073,741,824 bytes (binary/GiB).
gigabyte.history: Became ubiquitous in consumer technology in the 2000s with broadband internet, DVDs, and flash drives.
gigabyte.used_for: Smartphone RAM, hard drive space, HD video streaming, and mobile monthly data allowances.
examples: One hour of 1080p video streaming (~1.5–3 GB)
Smartphone RAM capacity (6 GB to 12 GB)

terabyte.definition: A unit of digital storage equal to 1,000,000,000,000 bytes (1,000 GB) or ~1.099×10¹² bytes (binary/TiB).
terabyte.history: First commercial 1 TB hard drive released by Hitachi in 2007, marking a milestone in data center storage density.
terabyte.used_for: External backup drives, cloud server capacity, 4K video editing, and database storage.
examples: Capacity of a typical external computer backup drive (1–2 TB)
Storage capacity for ~250,000 high-res digital photos

petabyte.definition: A unit of digital storage equal to 1,000 terabytes or 10¹⁵ bytes.
petabyte.history: Adopted by tech giants (Google, AWS, Meta) to describe big data infrastructure and internet traffic volumes.
petabyte.used_for: Data centers, AI model training datasets, web search indexes, and large scientific archives.
examples: Data generated by the Large Hadron Collider annually (~90 PB)
Estimated daily data processed by major search engines

joule.definition: The SI unit of energy, equal to the work done by a force of 1 newton acting through a distance of 1 meter.
joule.history: Named in honor of English physicist James Prescott Joule, who demonstrated the mechanical equivalent of heat in 1843.
joule.used_for: Physics kinetic/potential energy calculations, heat transfer, and mechanical work.
examples: Energy required to lift a small apple (100 g) 1 meter vertically (1 Joule)
Energy of an apple falling to ground

kilojoule.definition: A metric unit of energy equal to 1,000 joules.
kilojoule.history: Adopted internationally on dietary nutrition labels alongside or replacing the kilocalorie.
kilojoule.used_for: Food nutritional energy labeling (outside US), exercise energy expenditure, and chemical reactions.
examples: Recommended daily adult human food energy intake (~8,700 kJ)
Energy in a single slice of bread (~300–400 kJ)

calorie.definition: A unit of heat energy equal to the energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 gram of water by 1 °C (~4.184 Joules).
calorie.history: Introduced by French chemist Nicolas Clément in 1824 as a unit of heat in steam engine thermodynamics.
calorie.used_for: Chemistry lab calorimetry and thermodynamic physics problems.
examples: Heat needed to warm 1 mL of water by 1 °C (1 calorie)
Energy to heat a cup of tea by 10 °C (~2,500 cal)

kilocalorie.definition: A unit of energy equal to 1,000 small calories or ~4.184 kilojoules, commonly called a 'Dietary Calorie' (Cal).
kilocalorie.history: Adopted in food science to quantify metabolizable energy provided by carbohydrates, proteins, and fats.
kilocalorie.used_for: Food nutrition labels, calorie counting apps, and metabolic rate calculations.
examples: Average daily adult caloric requirement (~2,000 kcal / Calories)
Caloric content of a medium banana (~105 kcal)

watt-hour.definition: A unit of energy equal to 1 watt of power consumed continuously for 1 hour (3,600 joules).
watt-hour.history: Developed by electrical utility pioneers to bill customers based on steady power output over time.
watt-hour.used_for: Smartphone battery capacity ratings, laptop batteries, and small solar panel storage.
examples: Capacity of a typical laptop battery (~50–80 Wh)
Smartphone battery capacity (~15–20 Wh)

kilowatt-hour.definition: A unit of energy equal to 1,000 watt-hours or 3,600,000 joules (3.6 MJ).
kilowatt-hour.history: Standard billing unit used by electric utilities worldwide since the late 19th century.
kilowatt-hour.used_for: Monthly household electricity bills, electric vehicle battery pack capacity, and solar array output.
examples: Electricity used running a 1,000 W space heater for 1 hour (1 kWh)
Battery capacity of a Tesla Model 3 (~60–82 kWh)

electronvolt.definition: A unit of energy equal to the kinetic energy gained by a single electron accelerating through a 1-volt potential difference (~1.602×10⁻¹⁹ J).
electronvolt.history: Introduced in atomic physics to describe atomic orbital transitions and ionizing radiation.
electronvolt.used_for: Particle physics, semiconductor bandgap energies, chemical bond strength, and X-ray spectrum Analysis.
examples: Energy of visible light photons (~1.8–3.1 eV)
Binding energy of an electron in a hydrogen atom (13.6 eV)

btu.definition: British Thermal Unit — heat needed to raise the temperature of 1 pound of water by 1 °F (~1,055.06 Joules).
btu.history: Formulated in the UK in the late 19th century for steam engineering and thermal heating systems.
btu.used_for: Air conditioner cooling ratings, furnace heating output, and natural gas energy pricing.
examples: Cooling capacity of a bedroom window air conditioner (~8,000–12,000 BTU/hr)
Energy content of a standard wood match (~1 BTU)

watt.definition: The SI unit of power, equal to 1 joule per second (rate of energy transfer).
watt.history: Named after James Watt in 1882 to honor his contributions to steam engine development.
watt.used_for: Light bulb power ratings, consumer electronics, solar panel output, and audio speaker power.
examples: LED household light bulb (~9–12 W)
Kitchen microwave heating power (~800–1200 W)

kilowatt.definition: A unit of power equal to 1,000 watts (10³ W).
kilowatt.history: Standard industrial power unit adopted for rating electric motors and electrical generator capacity.
kilowatt.used_for: Electric vehicle motor power, home HVAC heating capacity, and industrial equipment.
examples: Electric motor output of a modern EV (~150–300 kW)
Power output of a residential rooftop solar system (~5–10 kW)

megawatt.definition: A unit of power equal to 1,000,000 watts (10⁶ W).
megawatt.history: Came into widespread use during the electrification of major cities and construction of utility power stations.
megawatt.used_for: Wind turbine generation capacity, power plant output, locomotive power, and aircraft carriers.
examples: Power generation capacity of a modern utility wind turbine (~2–5 MW)
Peak power of a diesel locomotive (~3 MW)

horsepower.definition: A unit of power equal to approximately 745.7 watts (mechanical horsepower).
horsepower.history: Coined by James Watt in 1782 to compare the output of steam engines against draft horses to sell his engines.
horsepower.used_for: Automotive engine power output, lawnmowers, boat outboard motors, and industrial pumps.
examples: Engine output of a standard sedan automobile (~150–250 hp)
Output of a typical riding lawnmower (~15–20 hp)

pascal.definition: The SI derived unit of pressure, equal to 1 newton per square meter (N/m²).
pascal.history: Named after French mathematician and physicist Blaise Pascal, known for his experiments with barometers.
pascal.used_for: Acoustic sound pressure, building ventilation pressure, materials science, and atmospheric physics.
examples: Pressure exerted by a single sheet of paper lying flat on a table (~1 Pa)
Human hearing threshold (~20 μPa)

kilopascal.definition: A unit of pressure equal to 1,000 pascals (0.01 bar).
kilopascal.history: Adopted in metric countries for meteorological barometric pressure, tire inflation, and blood pressure.
kilopascal.used_for: Vehicle tire pressure, meteorological isobar maps, and civil engineering soil mechanics.
examples: Standard atmospheric sea level pressure (~101.3 kPa)
Car tire inflation pressure (~200–240 kPa)

bar.definition: A metric unit of pressure equal to exactly 100,000 pascals (100 kPa), slightly less than 1 atm.
bar.history: Introduced by Norwegian meteorologist Vilhelm Bjerknes in 1909 to standardize weather pressure reporting.
bar.used_for: Scuba diving tank pressure, espresso machine extraction pressure, and industrial hydraulics.
examples: Standard espresso coffee extraction pressure (~9 bar)
Scuba diving air tank full pressure (~200 bar)

psi.definition: Pounds per Square Inch — pressure resulting from a 1-pound force applied over a 1-square-inch area (~6,894.76 Pa).
psi.history: Traditional imperial engineering unit developed during the industrial boiler revolution.
psi.used_for: Automobile tire pressure in US/UK, bicycle tires, air compressors, and hydraulic lines.
examples: Recommended passenger car tire pressure (~32–35 psi)
Road bicycle tire inflation pressure (~80–100 psi)

atmosphere.definition: A reference unit of pressure equal to 101,325 pascals or 14.696 psi (standard sea level pressure).
atmosphere.history: Established at the 10th General Conference on Weights and Measures (CGPM) in 1954 as a standard reference environment.
atmosphere.used_for: High-pressure physics, chemical reaction conditions, and deep-sea diving depths.
examples: Pressure felt at sea level on Earth (1 atm)
Water pressure at a ocean depth of 10 meters (~2 atm total)

torr.definition: A unit of pressure defined as exactly 1/760 of a standard atmosphere (~133.322 Pa), nearly equal to 1 mmHg.
torr.history: Named after Evangelista Torricelli, Italian physicist who invented the mercury barometer in 1643.
torr.used_for: High-vacuum physics, mass spectrometry, semiconductor vacuum chambers, and freeze-drying.
examples: High vacuum chamber pressure for microchip fabrication (~10⁻⁶ Torr)
Standard atmospheric pressure (~760 Torr)

degree.definition: A measurement of plane angle representing 1/360th of a full rotation.
degree.history: Traced to ancient Babylonian astronomy, which chose 360 based on their base-60 counting system and 365-day solar year.
degree.used_for: Geometry, map navigation compass headings, architecture, and carpentry angles.
examples: A right angle (90°)
Full circular turn (360°)

radian.definition: The SI unit of plane angle, equal to the angle subtended at the center of a circle by an arc equal in length to the radius (~57.2958°).
radian.history: Formally coined by mathematician James Thomson in 1873 to simplify calculus derivatives of trigonometric functions.
radian.used_for: Calculus, physics rotational dynamics, wave mechanics, and computer graphics shaders.
examples: Angle of a half-circle rotation (π radians / ~3.14159 rad)
Full circle rotation (2π radians / ~6.28318 rad)

gradian.definition: A unit of plane angle equal to 1/400th of a full circle (0.9 degrees).
gradian.history: Introduced during the French metric reform to make right angles exactly equal to 100 gradians.
gradian.used_for: Land surveying and civil engineering in parts of continental Europe.
examples: Right angle (100 gradians)
Full circle rotation (400 gradians)

arcminute.definition: A unit of angular measurement equal to 1/60th of a degree (1/21,600 of a circle).
arcminute.history: Developed by Ptolemy and ancient astronomers to measure small celestial separations in star catalogs.
arcminute.used_for: Telescope resolution, rifle scope adjustments (MOA), astronomy, and eye chart acuity tests.
examples: Angular diameter of the full Moon viewed from Earth (~31 arcminutes)
Human visual acuity threshold (~1 arcminute)

volt.definition: The SI derived unit of electric potential, electromotive force, and voltage (1 V = 1 W/A).
volt.history: Named in honor of Alessandro Volta, who constructed the first chemical electric battery (voltaic pile) in 1799.
volt.used_for: Battery voltage ratings, household power outlets, computer power supplies, and solar cells.
examples: Standard AA/AAA alkaline battery voltage (1.5 V)
Standard USB charging port output (5 V DC)

ampere.definition: The SI base unit of electric current. Defined by fixing the elementary charge e to 1.602176634×10⁻¹⁹ coulombs.
ampere.history: Named after French physicist André-Marie Ampère, father of classical electromagnetism.
ampere.used_for: Electrical circuit breaker ratings, battery charger output, electric motor draw, and welding current.
examples: Standard household circuit breaker capacity (15–20 A)
Smartphone fast-charger current output (~2–3 A)

ohm.definition: The SI derived unit of electrical resistance, equal to 1 volt per ampere (1 Ω = 1 V/A).
ohm.history: Named after Georg Simon Ohm, who published Ohm's Law (V = IR) in 1827.
ohm.used_for: Resistor electronic component values, speaker impedance, wire resistance, and circuit design.
examples: Impedance rating of standard home audio speakers (4 Ω or 8 Ω)
Resistance of a 100-watt incandescent light bulb (~144 Ω)

farad.definition: The SI unit of electrical capacitance, equal to 1 coulomb per volt (1 F = 1 C/V).
farad.history: Named after English scientist Michael Faraday, discoverer of electromagnetic induction and electrolysis.
farad.used_for: Capacitor electronic components, power supply filtering, energy storage, and touchscreens.
examples: Supercapacitor used for electric bus rapid charging (~500–3000 F)
Typical electronics decoupling capacitor (~100 μF)

henry.definition: The SI unit of electrical inductance, equal to 1 volt-second per ampere (1 H = 1 Wb/A).
henry.history: Named after American scientist Joseph Henry, who independently discovered electromagnetic induction in 1831.
henry.used_for: Transformers, electric motor windings, radio tuning inductors, and power chokes.
examples: Inductance of a power supply filter choke coil (~10–100 mH)
Small RF tuning inductor (~1–10 μH)

hertz.definition: The SI unit of frequency, equal to 1 cycle per second.
hertz.history: Named after German physicist Heinrich Hertz, who proved the existence of electromagnetic radio waves in 1887.
hertz.used_for: Audio sound frequencies, screen refresh rates, electrical AC grid frequency, and heart rate.
examples: Standard AC power grid frequency in North America (60 Hz)
High refresh rate gaming monitor (144 Hz)

kilohertz.definition: A unit of frequency equal to 1,000 cycles per second (10³ Hz).
kilohertz.history: Became important in early 20th century radio communications and audio signal processing.
kilohertz.used_for: AM radio broadcasts, audible human hearing range (20 Hz–20 kHz), and digital audio sampling.
examples: Standard CD-quality digital audio sampling rate (44.1 kHz)
Upper limit of human hearing (~20 kHz)

megahertz.definition: A unit of frequency equal to 1,000,000 cycles per second (10⁶ Hz).
megahertz.history: Defined early FM radio broadcasting bands and microprocessor clock speed benchmarks in the 1980s–1990s.
megahertz.used_for: FM radio channels, Wi-Fi bands (2.4 GHz / 5 GHz), medical MRI scanners, and bus speeds.
examples: FM radio broadcast frequency band (88 to 108 MHz)
Clock speed of early 1990s personal computers (~33–100 MHz)

gigahertz.definition: A unit of frequency equal to 1,000,000,000 cycles per second (10⁹ Hz).
gigahertz.history: Became critical in modern computing and microwave telecommunications in the late 1990s.
gigahertz.used_for: CPU clock frequencies, 5G cellular communications, satellite links, and microwave ovens.
examples: Clock frequency of a modern smartphone or PC CPU (~2.5–5.0 GHz)
Frequency of home Wi-Fi routers (2.4 GHz and 5 GHz)

becquerel.definition: The SI derived unit of radioactivity, equal to 1 radioactive decay per second.
becquerel.history: Named after French physicist Henri Becquerel, who discovered radioactivity in 1896 alongside Marie Curie.
becquerel.used_for: Nuclear physics, radioactive isotope decay rate measurement, and medical imaging isotopes.
examples: Radioactivity of natural potassium in a banana (~15 Bq)
Radioactivity of a human body (~4,000 Bq)

sievert.definition: The SI derived unit of ionizing radiation dose equivalent, measuring health effect on human tissue.
sievert.history: Named after Swedish medical physicist Rolf Sievert for his pioneering work on radiation dosage measurement.
sievert.used_for: Radiation safety limits, nuclear power plant monitoring, and medical X-ray dosimetry.
examples: Average annual natural background radiation dose (~2.4 mSv)
Single chest X-ray exposure (~0.1 mSv)

tesla.definition: The SI unit of magnetic flux density (1 T = 1 Wb/m² = 1 N/(A·m)).
tesla.history: Named in 1960 in honor of inventor Nikola Tesla for his contributions to alternating current and magnetic fields.
tesla.used_for: MRI medical scanners, particle accelerator magnets, and electric motor field strength.
examples: Earth's natural magnetic field at surface (~30–60 μT)
Clinical hospital MRI scanner magnet strength (1.5 T to 3.0 T)

lumen.definition: The SI unit of luminous flux, measuring total visible light emitted by a source in all directions.
lumen.history: Formulated in 1924 by the International Commission on Illumination (CIE) to replace outdated candlepower units.
lumen.used_for: Light bulb brightness ratings, video projector output, flashlights, and room lighting design.
examples: Brightness of a standard 60-watt equivalent LED light bulb (~800 lumens)
High-power tactical flashlight (~1,000–2,000 lumens)

lux.definition: The SI unit of illuminance, equal to 1 lumen per square meter (1 lx = 1 lm/m²).
lux.history: Adopted to quantify surface lighting levels for architectural illumination, photography, and safety.
lux.used_for: Office lighting standards, camera exposure light meters, greenhouse crop lighting, and streetlights.
examples: Recommended office desk task lighting level (~500 lux)
Direct bright sunlight at noon on a clear day (~100,000 lux)

candela.definition: The SI base unit of luminous intensity in a given direction. Defined by fixing the luminous efficacy of 540 THz monochromatic radiation to 683 lm/W.
candela.history: Evolved from historical 'candlepower', which was based on the light from a standard spermaceti candle.
candela.used_for: Lighthouse beam intensity, display screen brightness ratings (nits/cd/m²), and automotive headlights.
examples: Luminous intensity of a single wax candle in one direction (~1 candela)
Brightness of a smartphone OLED screen (~800–1000 cd/m²)
